extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, natural-law theory, and contract theory (readers of Hobbes' Leviathan)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and explicating the enumerated 'laws of nature' and related normative rules about rights, contracts, covenants, oaths, justice, and social cooperation as presented in Hobbes' Leviathan.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Fundamental Law of Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: "That every man, ought to endeavour Peace, as farre as he has hope of obtaining it; and when he cannot obtain it, that he may seek, and use, all helps, and advantages of Warre."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the first and fundamental precept: seek peace and follow it; only when peace cannot be obtained should one use means of war and defence. It frames all further rules of natural law.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Second Law of Nature (mutual renunciation of rights)
rubrics_metrics.description: "That a man be willing, when others are so too ... to lay down this right to all things; and be contented with so much liberty against other men, as he would allow other men against himselfe."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calls for reciprocal renunciation of unlimited natural rights to enable peace; links to the Golden Rule and the basis of covenant-making for mutual safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: What it is to lay down a right
rubrics_metrics.description: To lay downe a man's Right to anything is to devest himself of the Liberty of hindring another of the benefit of his own Right to the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that renouncing a right does not create a new right in another but removes obstacles so others may enjoy their original rights; emphasizes voluntary declaration (words/actions) as the mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renouncing vs Transferring Rights; Obligation and Justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Right is laid aside either by simply renouncing it (careth not to whom the benefit redoundeth) or by transferring it (intendeth the benefit to some certain person).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a right is renounced or transferred, the actor is obliged not to hinder the beneficiary; failure to respect such voluntary acts is injustice/injury (sine jure). Bonds (words/actions) bind mainly through fear of consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not all rights are alienable
rubrics_metrics.description: Some rights cannot be understood to be abandoned or transferred (e.g., the right to resist those who assault by force to take away life; to resist wounds, chains, imprisonment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because renouncing such rights would not aim at any good to oneself and because one cannot reliably interpret aggressors' intent, such rights remain inalienable. The motive is self-preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract defined (mutual transferring of right)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mutual transferring of Right is that which men call CONTRACT. Distinction between transferring a right and delivery of the thing itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contracts may involve immediate transfer and delivery (sale with ready money) or transfer now with delivery later; contract is voluntary and grounded in reciprocal benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covenant (promise and keeping faith)
rubrics_metrics.description: When one party delivers his part and leaves the other to perform later, trusted performance is called Covenant or Pact; keeping promise is Faith, failing is Violation of Faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covenants involve trust that one party will perform in the future; the concept links to obligations and the conditions under which promises bind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free-gift (non-mutual transfer)
rubrics_metrics.description: When transferring of Right is not mutual but given in hope of friendship, reputation, reward in heaven, etc., it is called Gift, Freegift, Grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Free-gifts create expectations of gratitude but are not contracts; the giver's motive is voluntary benefit to himself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of contract — express words
rubrics_metrics.description: Express signs are words spoken with understanding of their signification (present, past, or future tenses). Words of the future are called promises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporal form of words matters for legal effect: present/past words can transfer future rights; words of the future (bare promise) are generally insufficient for a free-gift unless other signs of intent exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of contract — inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs by inference include consequences of words, silence, actions, or forbearing an action; any sufficiently clear indication of will may indicate contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-verbal behavior can constitute contractual assent when it sufficiently demonstrates the contractor's will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free gift passes by words of the present or past
rubrics_metrics.description: Words of the present/past (e.g., 'I have given' or 'I do give') can transfer a future right by virtue of present intention, whereas bare future words usually do not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains difference between expressing a present will that affects future rights versus merely promising a future act; exceptions occur when other signs show intent (e.g., prize for a race).

rubrics_metrics.name: Promise can be equivalent to covenant in contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: In buying, selling, and other acts of contract, a promise may be equivalent to a covenant when one party has already received the benefit for which the promise is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a person performs first, the promise given after may be taken as transferring right because performance would not otherwise occur; thus promises can be obligatory in many contractual contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit (deserving from performance)
rubrics_metrics.description: He that performeth first in a contract is said to merit that which he is to receive; in contests/prizes, winners 'merit' by virtue of the propounding of the prize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes contractual merit (due by contractors) from merit from gifts (dependent on giver's benignity); connects to scholastic distinctions (meritum congrui vs condigni) and to rewards like Paradise as a contested analogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covenants of mutual trust are void without common power
rubrics_metrics.description: If a covenant is made wherein neither party performs presently but trust one another in the condition of mere Nature, it is void; unless a common Power exists to compel performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In absence of coercive authority, the fear of being betrayed makes mutual-trust covenants invalid; performing first without assurance is self-betrayal unless enforcement exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to the end contains right to the means
rubrics_metrics.description: He that transferreth any Right, transferreth the Means of enjoying it, as farre as lyeth in his power (e.g., sale of land understood to transfer herbage; sovereignty implies right to levy money for soldiers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transfers of rights are interpreted to include necessary means to enjoy those rights; practical implications for interpretation of transfers of sovereignty, property, and fixtures.

rubrics_metrics.name: No covenant with brute beasts
rubrics_metrics.description: To make Covenant with brute Beasts is impossible because they do not understand our speech nor accept translations of Right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mutual acceptance is required for covenant; animals cannot be parties to covenants.

rubrics_metrics.name: No covenant with God without special revelation
rubrics_metrics.description: To make Covenant with God is impossible except by mediation of those God speaks to (revelation) or by his lieutenants; otherwise we do not know whether covenants are accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vows contrary to the law of nature are vain; if commanded by the law of nature, the law, not the vow, is binding.

rubrics_metrics.name: No covenant but of possible and future things
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject of a Covenant must be deliberable and something to come judged possible to perform; promising what is known impossible is no covenant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If something promised becomes impossible later, the covenant binds to its value or to sincere endeavour to perform what is possible; obligations cannot require impossible acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: How covenants are discharged
rubrics_metrics.description: Men are freed of their Covenants either by Performing or by being Forgiven (restitution of liberty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance is the natural end of obligation; forgiveness restores the right previously transferred and frees the obligor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covenants extorted by fear are valid
rubrics_metrics.description: Covenants entered into by fear (e.g., paying ransom for life) in the condition of mere Nature are obligatory; prisoners of war bound to pay ransom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where no other law forbids performance, a covenant made under compulsion to preserve life binds until civil law discharges it; fear does not automatically void a covenant.

rubrics_metrics.name: A former covenant to one makes void a later to another
rubrics_metrics.description: A former Covenant makes void a later one: having passed away his Right to one today, it cannot pass tomorrow to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chronology and prior transfer control the availability of rights for subsequent promises; later promises that attempt to pass already-transferred rights are null.

rubrics_metrics.name: A covenant not to defend oneself is void
rubrics_metrics.description: A Covenant not to defend oneself from force by force is always void: no man can transfer the right to save himself from death, wounds, or imprisonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promises to forgo self-defence are unenforceable because they would abandon the primary end of conserving life; authorities still execute criminals with armed guards despite their prior consent to the law.

rubrics_metrics.name: No man obliged to accuse himself
rubrics_metrics.description: A Covenant to accuse oneself without assurance of pardon is invalid; in the state of nature there is no place for accusation; in civil society accusation leads to punishment and thus to resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testimony given under coercion or torture is unreliable; one is not bound to give self-accusatory testimony that would lead to one's own punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and force of an oath
rubrics_metrics.description: An Oath is a form of speech added to a promise signifying that unless he perform, he renounceth the mercy of God or calleth Him for vengeance; oath takes place by the God the swearer thinks God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oaths strengthen covenants by invoking fear of divine vengeance and social shame; an oath adds nothing to the moral force of a lawful covenant and is vain if not according to the swearer's religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: An oath adds nothing to the obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: A Covenant, if lawful, binds in the sight of God without the Oath, as much as with it; if unlawful, it binds not at all though confirmed with an oath.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oaths do not create obligations beyond the underlying legality/validity of the covenant; they are rhetorical/religious reinforcement rather than constitutive.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Third Law of Nature: Justice (perform covenants)
rubrics_metrics.description: "That Men Performe Their Covenants Made": the definition of injustice is the not-performance of covenant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice originates in the obligation to keep valid covenants; without covenants there is no propriety and thus no injustice (state of war).

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice and propriety begin with constitution of commonwealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Before a coercive power (commonwealth) exists there is no propriety and thus no injustice; justice as keeping covenants presupposes a power to compel performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishment of civil power is necessary to make covenants valid in practice and to create property and distributive arrangements enforceable by punishment greater than benefit of breach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice is consonant with reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Keeping of covenant is a rule of reason by which we are forbidden to do anything destructive to our life; justice is not contrary to reason even when the breach appears beneficial in some rare specious cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues against the view that success by unjust means can be rational; breach of covenant undermines society and personal security, thus contradicting reason aimed at self-preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covenants not discharged by vice of the covenantee
rubrics_metrics.description: Exceptions claiming certain persons (heretics, habitual covenant-breakers) discharge covenants are against reason; faults of a person that would discharge a covenant should have been known to prevent making it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One cannot rationally rely on a covenant if one expects the covenantee's vice at the time of contracting; hypocrisy cannot retroactively void a covenant reasonably made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice of men (manners) vs justice of actions
rubrics_metrics.description: When attributed to men, justice signifies conformity of manners to reason; when attributed to actions, it signifies conformity of particular actions to reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes a just person (habitual disposition) from a guiltless action; allows for a just person to err and for an unjust disposition to sometimes act rightly by accident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nothing done to a man by his own consent can be injury
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatsoever is done to a man conformable to his own Will signified to the doer is no Injury to him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consent negates injury unless antecedent rights have not been properly transferred; expressed will can release claims of injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commutative and distributive justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Commutative justice pertains to equality of value in contracts (arithmetic proportion); distributive justice pertains to distribution of equal benefit to men of equal merit (geometric proportion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes argues the common scholastic exposition is imperfect: commutative justice concerns performance of contracts; distributive justice (properly equity) concerns arbitrators defining what is just.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Fourth Law of Nature: Gratitude
rubrics_metrics.description: "That a man which receiveth Benefit from another of meer Grace, Endeavour that he which giveth it, have no reasonable cause to repent him of his good will."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reciprocity for gratuitous benefits prevents erosion of benevolence; ingratitude is the breach of this natural rule analogous to injustice for covenants.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Fifth Law of Nature: Mutual accommodation (compleasance)
rubrics_metrics.description: "That every man strive to accommodate himselfe to the rest."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promotes social smoothness: individuals should adapt and avoid asperity that hinders social building; stubbornness that retains others' necessities for superfluities threatens social cohesion and peace.
